meta.title: French Bulldog breathing and heat problems
meta.description: Learn to manage Frenchie breathing, heat, and warning signs with episode, temperature, and activity tracking.
meta.keywords: frenchie breathing problems, french bulldog BOAS, french bulldog heat stroke

hero.headline: Frenchies do not just “breathe weird”: they have a condition you can manage
hero.subhead: Your Frenchie is not broken. They are built differently.
hero.body: The snoring, snorting, and panting can be scary. In Frenchies, the flat face changes airflow and heat regulation. The goal is not to live afraid. It is to know what to watch, when to slow down, and when to call the vet.

items.question: My Frenchie snores loudly, so it is normal
items.answer: It is common, but changes in intensity, awake snoring, or visible effort should be tracked and discussed.

items.question: If they pant, they just exercised
items.answer: It can be heat, stress, or breathing effort. Room temperature matters as much as activity.

items.question: Frenchies cannot exercise
items.answer: They can move, but need short sessions, controlled weather, and frequent breaks.

items.question: If they breathe well at the vet, they are fine
items.answer: Many episodes happen at home, in heat, or after play. History shows what the vet did not see.

items.question: There is nothing to do about BOAS
items.answer: There is a lot to manage: weight, weather, activity, alerts, and informed veterinary decisions.

emergency.title: These signs need a vet immediately
items: Blue, gray, or very pale gums
Labored breathing that does not improve at rest

solution.title: Understand when it happens, not only that it happened.
solution.body: Frenchie Care tracks episodes, temperature, humidity, duration, prior activity, and recovery. Over time you see the map: safer days, routines that trigger panting, and signs worth discussing.
bullets: Correlation with walks, play, and rest

footer.tagline: Calm, data, and responsible decisions for Frenchies.
footer.disclaimer: Frenchie Care does not replace veterinary attention. For emergency signs, seek immediate help.
